Section 1

Job Margin Overview

In 2025, the shop earned $56.1M of revenue from 4,355 jobs. It earned $14.2M of gross margin (revenue less variable production costs and overhead), a 25.4% rate. This actual margin was 3.4 percentage points lower than the 28.8% rate the shop's estimates promised as actual job costs came in $852K over the jobs' estimates.

At the job-level, the average margin was 21.2% in 2025 against the 26.8% estimates. Larger jobs carry a higher margin, which is why the shop's total margin was 4.2 percentage points higher than the job-level average. In the distribution below, we see that 2,390 jobs (55% of total) had margins above the 21.2% average and 1,965 jobs (45%) were below it, while 322 jobs (7.4%) lost money. The second chart shows each job's actual margin less its estimated margin: 63% of jobs came in below their estimate, by a median of 9 points, and the red bars are the 13% more than 20 points below.

2025 Job Margin Distribution
2025 Actual vs. Estimated Job Margin

Jobs on repeat parts carry a higher average margin than new quoted work (23.2% versus 19.1%). At the same time, jobs on repeat parts missed their margin estimates more frequently than new quoted work (68.8% vs 53.0%), and the magnitude of the miss was also greater (7.1 points vs 2.9). Jobs on both repeat parts and new quoted work lost money at similar rates, 6.9% and 8.4%, respectively. A repeat part's estimate comes from its original quote, and as this report details, underestimates the movements in material, rates and standards since then; a new part's estimate is weeks old.

2025 Job Margin, by Job Type
2025 Actual vs. Estimated Job Margin, by Job Type

There are significant margin differences between jobs of different sizes. Jobs with lots under 25 pieces average 13.6% margin and lose money on 19.3% of them; lots of 25 to 100 pieces average 22.4% margin and lose money on 5.7%, and lots over 100 pieces average 24.2% margin and lose money on 2.6%. The small lots also miss their estimates by the most, an average of 11.6 points against 4.7 and 2.9. The primary driver for this is that setup hours, which are consistent across jobs, have a larger impact on small jobs' lower revenue.

Section 2

Job Cost Overruns

As shown above, actual job margin was consistently lower than estimated. The reason for this is that the actual job costs overrun in 2025 was $852K. As the chart below shows, the primary drivers were outside processing and run hours.

Actual Cost against Estimate on the 2025 Jobs, by Element

A significant portion of this $852K cost overrun is from cost elements not being included in the quote ($344K total; $220K of outside processing and $124K of scrap and rework).

Of the remaining $508K:

  • Run hours came in $208K over estimate on net, with the median job at 1.08× its estimated run hours.
  • Outside processing came in $301K over on net; on the 3,181 jobs with both an estimate and a purchase order, invoices came to 1.05× the estimates.
  • Setup hours came in $17K over on net: the median job took 1.59× its estimated setup on a part's first run after a revision (versus 0.84× on a part run within the year).

Section 3

Blended Rate Adjustments

The shop's existing quote system costed every labor hour at one blended shop rate, $178 in 2025 and $185 in 2026. The work-center pools, as set in May 2026, run from $102 an hour at deburr to $277 at the 5-axis cell.

Work-center Pool Rates against the Blended Shop Rate

The chart below shows the impact on reported vs. actual margin by part family after accounting for differences in work-center pool rates. Costed at the pools, the families that run on the manual and secondary cells gain margin vs. their reported figures (Fixtures and tooling +6.6 points, Weldments and assemblies +6.5) and the families that run on the more expensive cells lose margin vs. their reported figures (Aerospace brackets -7.4, Turbine components -2.9). Aerospace brackets is the shop's highest margin part family at the blended rate and number 8 of 11 at the pools.

Margin by Part Family at the Blended Rate and at the Pool Rates, 2025 Jobs

The blended rate left $902K of cost out of the 2 families it underpriced, $1.15M at the markup price, and overstated the cost of the other 9 by $1.41M (96% of the cost measured). This is what the "labor rate" movements in the repricing queue are.

Section 4

Jobs that Lost Money

322 jobs lost money in 2025, $224.2K in total (95% of the cost measured). Only 32 of them were estimated to lose money before they started. The other 290 were estimated to make money, at a median estimated margin of 22%, and lost it during the job; they account for 74% of the loss. Each job carries the driver the reporting layer assigns by rule, and the action the driver maps to. On 78 jobs, $41.7K of the $224.2K, no single driver accounts for most of the overrun; those jobs are accepted as one-offs and are left out of the chart of loss by driver below.

Loss making jobs by driver

The chart shows the loss carried by each driver, with the number of jobs behind it. A routing standard the part's jobs keep overrunning carries 45% of the loss on 101 jobs; together with prices set below estimated cost, setups on new or infrequent parts and vendor rates, the drivers that sit with the estimator carry 57% of the loss. The drivers that sit with the floor and the front office, unbilled revision work, scrap and rework and material, carry 24%.

Loss on the 244 Loss-making Jobs with a Driver, 2025

Estimated margin against the margin earned

Each dot is one loss-making job, placed by the margin the estimate promised and the margin the job earned. Dots left of the vertical line were expected to lose money; the rest were not. The routing-standard jobs were estimated at a median margin of 20% and fell a median of 29 points, half of them between 19 and 40 points. The change-order jobs fell the furthest of the five actions, a median of 40 points, which is one revision's work absorbed on one job. The 32 jobs priced to lose money lost a median of $177, against $277 on the 290.

The 322 Loss-making Jobs by Action, 2025

Parts that lost money more than once

36 parts lost money on two or more releases in 2025; they account for 79 jobs and $93.8K of the loss. The chart shows the fifteen largest, with how many of the part's 2025 releases lost money and the driver behind them. A part that lost money on 4 of 5 releases is a standard or a price that is wrong, not a bad day, and the list is where the estimator starts. On 8 of the 15 the driver is the same on every loss-making release.

The Fifteen Parts with the Largest Loss over Two or More Releases

How concentrated the loss is

The line shows the share of the $224.2K reached as jobs are added from the largest loss down. The 25 largest losses carry 52% of the total and half of the loss sits in 23 jobs, so the review list is short. Of the 25 largest, 9 trace to a routing standard the part's jobs keep overrunning, 4 to unbilled revision work and 3 to prices set below their own estimated cost; 7 fire no rule with a dominant share and are accepted as one-offs, and the other 2 carry other drivers.
